newsitem.title: UK: Rate rise hits UK house mkt more than budget - CEBR.
newsitem.headline: Rate rise hits UK house mkt more than budget - CEBR.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown's first budget did little to restrain Britain's housing market but Thursday's rate rise will have more effect, the Centre for Economics and Business Research said.

Douglas McWilliams, the CEBR's chief executive, said budget measures, including a cut in mortgage interest relief from 15 percent to 10 percent and the increase in stamp duty on houses worth more than 250,000 stg, would cut the price of an average house by just 88 pounds.
"That is an insignificant amount given that the average house price is rising by about 7,000 stg a year at present," he said.

Stamp duty, currently levied at one percent on all house purchases, will rise to 1.5 percent for houses worth a quarter of a million pounds or more and to two percent on houses worth more than 500,000.
But McWilliams said the quarter-point rise in base rates, announced by the Bank of England on Thursday, taking them to 6.75 percent, would cut the average house price by a further 228 pounds.
"We expect that by the time the current interest rate cycle is over, higher interest rates will have slowed house price inflation to about three percent," McWilliams said.
"That will cut price increases by about 5,400 pounds a year compared with what might have happened if the present rate of increase of about 10 percent were to continue."
But the problem with using interest rates as the main policy weapon is that exporters and the corporate sector in general will continue to suffer from a strong pound, he said.
